title: Pipes, grep, and reading logs
objective: By the end of this lesson you can chain small commands together to answer a real question from a log file — the core working skill of anyone who investigates systems.

blocks.text: This is the capstone, and it is where the Unix idea finally pays off. Each command you have learned does one narrow thing. The power comes from connecting them: the output of one becomes the input of the next, and a question nobody wrote a tool for gets answered in a single line.
Every command has an input, an output, and a separate channel for errors. You redirect them with a small set of symbols.

rows: Send the output of the left command into the right command
Write output to a file, replacing what was there
Append output to the end of a file

blocks.alt: A pipeline of four commands. cat access.log emits every line, grep filters to only the failures, cut keeps just the path field, and sort with uniq counts them. The result is a short list such as 12 slash admin slash login.
blocks.caption: Each step reads the previous step's output. Stop anywhere and look — that is how you debug one.

blocks.title: > overwrites without asking
blocks.text: command > results.txt destroys whatever results.txt held. >> adds to it. This is the same lesson as rm, in a different costume: the shell does exactly what you said, immediately.
The four commands that do most of the work

blocks.caption: Your investigation toolkit
lines: grep 'pattern' file       # print only lines that match
grep -c 'error' file      # count matches instead of printing them
grep -v 'healthcheck' f   # invert: everything EXCEPT matches
uniq -c                   # collapse duplicates and count them

blocks.text: Here is a question a real person gets asked: which IP addresses failed to log in, and which one tried hardest? There is no single command for that. There is a pipeline.

blocks.caption: Read it left to right, as a sentence
lines: grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
#   -> pull out the IP address field
#      -> sort them so identical ones sit together
#            -> sort by that count, highest first

blocks.text: Each stage is simple and replaceable. If the log format differs on your system, you change one stage rather than looking for a different tool. That composability is the whole design philosophy, and it is why these commands have outlived every product built to replace them.

rows: Everything else, often one directory per service
On systemd machines, logs for one specific service

blocks.title: Reading auth.log is a real security skill
blocks.text: Failed passwords, sudo commands, new sessions from unfamiliar addresses — the evidence for most host-level questions is sitting in that one file. Being able to interrogate it with a pipeline, on a machine with no security tooling installed, is the difference between waiting for a dashboard and finding the answer.

blocks.title: Answer a question with a pipeline
steps: Run: sudo grep -c 'sudo' /var/log/auth.log          (how many sudo events)
Run: sudo grep 'sudo' /var/log/auth.log | tail -5   (the most recent ones)
Run: ls /var/log | wc -l                            (how many log files exist)
Run: sudo journalctl -n 20                          (last 20 system journal entries, if systemd)
Build your own: pick any log and count how many lines mention a word you choose
blocks.expected: Counts and recent entries from your own machine's authentication log, then a pipeline you assembled yourself. If your distribution stores authentication elsewhere, finding that out is part of the exercise.

blocks.text: You now have the foundation the rest of security work is built on: you know what the operating system is doing, you can move around it, you can read and set permissions, you can see what is running, and you can interrogate a log. Every next topic — networking, hardening, incident response, cloud — assumes exactly this and adds to it.

blocks.title: The habit that matters most
blocks.text: When something on a Linux machine confuses you, the answer is almost always available from the machine itself: a man page, a config file in /etc, a log in /var/log, or a process list. Reach for those before reaching for a search engine. That habit is what makes someone able to work on a system they have never seen.

cheatsheet: | pipes output into the next command · > overwrites a file · >> appends · 2> redirects errors
grep finds lines · -i ignores case · -c counts · -v inverts
wc -l counts lines · sort orders · uniq -c collapses and counts
sort | uniq -c | sort -rn = the standard 'what is most frequent' pattern
/var/log/auth.log holds logins, sudo use and failures
journalctl -u <service> reads one service's logs on systemd
Change one stage of a pipeline rather than looking for a different tool
The machine can usually answer your question about itself: man, /etc, /var/log, ps

choices.A: Runs two commands at the same time independently
choices.B: Sends the output of the command on the left as the input of the command on the right
choices.D: Comments out the rest of the line

checkpoint.explanation: That connection is the whole idea: small single-purpose commands become an answer when chained.

checkpoint.prompt: You want to append results to an existing file without destroying it. Which do you use?
checkpoint.explanation: > replaces the file's contents outright. >> adds to the end. 2> redirects errors, and | pipes to a command, not a file.

checkpoint.prompt: Which pipeline answers "which values appear most often, highest first"?
checkpoint.explanation: uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates, so you sort first, count with uniq -c, then sort numerically in reverse to rank them.

checkpoint.prompt: On a Debian or Ubuntu machine, where do you look for failed login attempts?
checkpoint.explanation: Authentication events — logins, failures, and sudo use — go to /var/log/auth.log. /etc/passwd lists accounts, which is a different question.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is a pipeline often preferable to finding a purpose-built tool for the same question?

choices.B: Each stage is simple and replaceable, so a change in the data means editing one stage rather than needing a different tool — and it works on any machine without installing anything
choices.C: Purpose-built tools cannot read log files

checkpoint.explanation: Composability and availability. The commands are already on the machine, and adapting the pipeline is a smaller change than adopting new software.
